summary: Summarizes the key features of BGP and analyzes the protocol with respect to scaling and performance. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This reviews how well the system for telling networks about each other will work as the Internet grows.

questions: how much bandwidth does bgp use
subtitle: How the BGP routing protocol scales as the Internet grows

tldr.problem: As the Internet grows, routing protocols must be able to handle exponentially more networks without consuming excessive bandwidth, memory, or CPU cycles.
tldr.mechanism: BGP is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol that uses path attributes to track the full path taken by routes, incremental updates to conserve bandwidth, and TCP for reliable transport. Its design separates the initial routing exchange from ongoing updates, and path attributes enable policy-based routing.
tldr.outcome: BGP's scaling properties depend on network stability rather than the total number of networks, allowing it to work well in large heterogeneous Internets. Its architecture proved flexible enough to become the de facto standard for connecting autonomous systems.

today: RFC 1265 is an Informational RFC providing performance analysis of BGP in 1991. BGP has since become the universal standard for inter-domain routing on the Internet and continues to scale as the number of networks has grown from thousands to hundreds of thousands.

sections.title: BGP as an Inter-Autonomous System Protocol
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is designed for routing between autonomous systems (AS)—independently operated networks that make their own routing decisions. BGP is not responsible for routing within an autonomous system (that job belongs to interior gateway protocols); instead, BGP carries routing information between autonomous systems.

BGP comes in multiple versions. Version 1 was published in RFC 1105, Version 2 in RFC 1163, and Version 3 (the subject of this analysis) in RFC 1267. The main changes from Version 1 to Version 2 were the introduction of path attributes and a cleaner message format. Version 3 made only minor refinements.

This document analyzes BGP's performance and scalability to determine whether it meets the criteria for advancement to Draft Standard status.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is the system that routers at the edge of different networks use to tell each other which networks they can reach.

sections.title: Key Features and Algorithm
sections.content:
BGP's design reflects a hybrid approach to routing. Like a distance-vector protocol, it exchanges only the routes currently in use rather than complete topology information. Like a link-state protocol, it can reconstruct portions of the overall Internet topology because each routing update carries the full AS-PATH—the sequence of autonomous systems the route has traversed.

The AS-PATH is one of the most important path attributes. Path attributes are metadata attached to each route, partitioned into well-known attributes (understood by all BGP speakers) and optional attributes (allowing experimentation). This structure gives BGP flexibility: new optional attributes can be added without breaking existing implementations, much like options in the Telnet protocol.

After the initial exchange of routing information between two BGP speakers, the protocol uses incremental updates—only changes are exchanged, not the entire routing table. This conserves bandwidth and CPU cycles. To ensure these incremental updates arrive reliably, BGP runs over TCP, which provides ordered, reliable delivery.

BGP also allows for graceful coexistence with the older EGP protocol and supports statically defined routes.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP sends the full path of networks a route has taken, which helps prevent loops, and later only sends changes to that list rather than re-sending everything.

sections.title: Bandwidth and Memory Scaling
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes BGP's resource consumption by modeling the Internet with key variables: N (total networks), M (mean AS distance), A (total autonomous systems), and K (peers per router).

During the initial connection between two BGP speakers, the worst-case bandwidth consumed is roughly O(N + M * A) bytes. For a typical 1991 Internet snapshot (2,100 networks, 59 ASes, mean distance 5), this is about 9,000 bytes. As the Internet grows, even with 100,000 networks, the initial exchange is only about 520,000 bytes.

After initial exchange, if the network is stable, BGP consumes only keepalive messages (19 octets every 30 seconds, about 5 bits/sec). If the network is unstable and routes change frequently, bandwidth consumption is O(C * M), where C is the number of route changes per second. Crucially, this depends on change frequency, not the total number of networks.

For memory, worst-case requirements scale as O((N + M * A) * K). In NSFNET in 1991 with 2,100 networks, the overhead of path attributes compared to the older EGP protocol was less than 7 percent.

The RFC concludes that BGP has no scaling problems in bandwidth and CPU utilization as the Internet grows, provided network stability is maintained. Memory scaling is dominated by N (number of networks) times K (peers per router), which is unavoidable with any routing protocol using the flat IP address space.
sections.plainLanguage: Starting a connection takes space that grows slowly with network size, ongoing maintenance uses just a tiny bit of bandwidth, and the memory needed grows mainly with the number of networks times the number of neighbors.

sections.title: What BGP Is Well Suited For
sections.content:
BGP is designed for the "hop-by-hop" routing paradigm used in the Internet, where each router makes independent forwarding decisions based on what its neighbors tell it. This paradigm supports any policy that can be enforced by applying local rules at each autonomous system.

The RFC documents that BGP is well suited for the current Internet and is nearly a necessity: the older EGP protocol imposed unjustifiable topological restrictions, handled information exchange inefficiently, and suffered from severe routing instabilities. BGP provides flexible mechanisms for policy-based routing through path attributes while maintaining simplicity.

The protocol was designed with flexibility and expandability in mind: it includes only essential functionality while providing mechanisms to extend behavior through optional attributes. Examples of such extensions already in use include repairing partitioned autonomous systems.

Whether BGP is suitable for other networking paradigms (non-hop-by-hop routing, non-IP protocols, or different topologies) is an open question the RFC does not attempt to answer.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP works well for how the Internet routes packets today, and it is much better than the older system, but it would need changes to work in very different kinds of networks.
